paragraphs.text: Figure 3: The Changing Accuracy using pruning methods

related_claims.content: Fine-grained layer-wise pruning, when applied without fine-tuning, yields larger accuracy drops than global unstructured pruning.
When followed by fine-tuning, fine-grained layer-wise pruning can recover or surpass baseline accuracy on structurally sensitive tasks.
On tasks other than structurally sensitive tasks, fine-grained pruning with fine-tuning does not recover baseline accuracy at high sparsity.
Global pruning is lower-variance than fine-grained pruning.
Global pruning is safer for general compression than fine-grained pruning.
Fine-grained pruning is higher-variance than global pruning.
Fine-grained pruning may preserve critical substructures.
Fine-grained pruning may yield better accuracy recovery than global pruning on some datasets.

Layer-wise analysis of sparsity under global unstructured magnitude pruning applied to the GNN architectures (GNNNet on BBBP, SplineConv on Cora node classification, HGP-SL on Proteins) reveals heterogeneous sensitivity to pruning.
Global pruning is more energy-efficient than fine-grained pruning at medium-to-high sparsities.

In experiments applying the evaluated pruning and fine-tuning workflows to the GNN architectures (SplineConv, NESS, HGP-SL, GNNNet, GIN) and datasets (Cora, Proteins, BBBP), no such subnetwork as that described in note 1, note 2 was found.

In experiments applying the evaluated pruning and fine-tuning workflows to the GNN architectures (SplineConv, NESS, HGP-SL, GNNNet, GIN) and datasets (Cora, Proteins, BBBP), smaller subnetworks obtained by the evaluated pruning schedules generally failed to match full-model accuracy without careful task- and layer-specific tuning.

The lottery ticket hypothesis (LTH), as tested here—in the experiments applying the evaluated pruning and fine-tuning workflows to the GNN architectures (SplineConv, NESS, HGP-SL, GNNNet, GIN) and datasets (Cora, Proteins, BBBP)—is not supported for these graph models and tasks.

In the comparison of the two magnitude-based pruning methods applied to the GNN architectures (SplineConv, NESS, HGP-SL, GNNNet, GIN) and tasks (node classification on Cora, link prediction on Cora, graph classification on BBBP and Proteins), global unstructured pruning exhibits more consistent behavior across tasks than fine-grained layer-wise pruning.
On the two graph classification tasks on BBBP and Proteins, fine-grained pruning with fine-tuning does not recover baseline accuracy at high sparsity.
For global pruning, CPU usage peaks at 70% sparsity across Cora node classification, Cora link prediction, BBBP, and Proteins.
Global pruning is more energy-efficient than fine-grained pruning at the sparsity values of 0.4–0.8.
Global unstructured pruning tolerates moderate sparsity (30–60%) with small accuracy degradation.
Global unstructured pruning does not require per-layer tuning.
For fine-grained pruning, energy consumption is higher than for global pruning at low-to-moderate sparsities.
For fine-grained pruning, energy consumption is higher than for global pruning at the sparsity values of 0.1–0.3.
Global unstructured magnitude pruning on the Cora node classification setup shows accuracy recovering from values near 0.86 to 0.90 ± 0.01 after fine-tuning at certain pruning levels.
For global pruning, CPU usage peaks at 70% sparsity across datasets.
Accuracy after pruning often remains near baseline or improves following fine-tuning.
Early convolutional layers exhibit tolerance to pruning even at high global sparsity targets.
When followed by fine-tuning, fine-grained layer-wise pruning can recover or surpass baseline accuracy on the structurally sensitive node classification task on Cora.

Both global unstructured magnitude pruning, which applies a uniform sparsity ratio across all weights, and fine-grained layer-wise magnitude pruning, which applies per-layer magnitude thresholds, substantially reduce on-disk model size when the model state is stored sparsely by keeping only nonzero weight values and their positions.
For fine-grained pruning, CPU and energy consumption exhibit sharp spikes and bimodal profiles.

The effects described in claim 1, claim 2, claim 4 were observed across the evaluated GNN architectures (SplineConv, NESS, HGP-SL, GNNNet, GIN) and datasets (Cora, Proteins, BBBP). [Referenced claim 1: Both global unstructured magnitude pruning, which applies a uniform sparsity ratio across all weights, and fine-grained layer-wise magnitude pruning, which applies per-layer magnitude thresholds, substantially reduce on-disk model size when the model state is stored sparsely by keeping only nonzero weight values and their positions.] [Referenced claim 2: Empirically, pruned models achieve size reductions of approximately 4–9× at high sparsity (80–90%), depending on dataset and method.] [Referenced claim 4: Accuracy after pruning often remains near baseline or improves following fine-tuning.]
Linear projection layers and final classifier MLPs exhibit greater sensitivity to pruning than early convolutional layers.
In the experiments on GNN architectures and datasets, reductions in parameter count from pruning did not translate into consistent decreases in inference time or memory usage.
